dnieper-donets-culture.name: Dnieper–Donets culture
dnieper-donets-culture.summary: A Mesolithic and Neolithic archaeological culture found north of the Black Sea, dating to about 5000–4200 BCE.

yamnaya-culture.name: Yamnaya culture
yamnaya-culture.summary: A Copper to early Bronze Age culture of the Pontic–Caspian steppe (3300–2600 BC), known for pit-grave burials under kurgans and often linked to Proto-Indo-European origins.

david-w-anthony.name: David W. Anthony
david-w-anthony.summary: American anthropologist specializing in horse domestication and Indo-European migrations, known for his book The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007).

pontic-caspian-steppe.name: Pontic–Caspian Steppe
pontic-caspian-steppe.summary: A vast grassland stretching from the northern Black Sea to the Caspian Sea, corresponding to ancient Scythia and Sarmatia, and thought to be where horses were first domesticated.

idel-ural.name: Volga-Ural region
idel-ural.summary: A historical region in Eastern Europe around the Volga and Ural rivers, in what is today Russia, now encompassing six republics including Tatarstan and Bashkortostan.

mikhailovka-culture.name: Mikhailovka culture
mikhailovka-culture.summary: A Copper Age archaeological culture (3600–3000 BCE) on the Pontic steppe, named for a fortified site in Ukraine, linked to the origins of the Yamnaya culture.

comb-ceramic-culture.name: Comb Ceramic culture
comb-ceramic-culture.summary: A northeast European culture, roughly 4200 to 2000 BCE, marked by pit-comb pottery and a mostly hunter-gatherer lifestyle with some early farming.

cucuteni-trypillia-culture.name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
cucuteni-trypillia-culture.summary: A Neolithic–Chalcolithic farming culture, about 5050 to 2950 BC, in southeast Europe whose 'mega-site' settlements, some with thousands of structures, were among the largest in the world at the time.

proto-indo-europeans.name: Proto-Indo-Europeans
proto-indo-europeans.summary: A prehistoric Eurasian people, likely living in the Pontic-Caspian steppe between about 6400 and 3500 BC, whose descendants spread across Eurasia including the Hittites and Mycenaean Greeks.

volosovo-culture.name: Volosovo culture
volosovo-culture.summary: An archaeological culture of forest foragers around the middle Volga and Kama basin, emerging between the 4th and 3rd millennium BC and lasting into the 2nd millennium BC.

kemi-oba-culture.name: Kemi Oba culture
kemi-oba-culture.summary: An archaeological culture (c. 3700–2200 BC) near the Sea of Azov and the lower Bug, Dnieper and Crimea, overlapping with the Catacomb culture.

netted-ware-culture.name: Netted Ware culture
netted-ware-culture.summary: A Bronze Age culture, also called the Textile Ceramic culture, spanning northeastern Europe from Finland to Russia's upper Volga region.

kurgan.name: Kurgan
kurgan.summary: A type of burial mound built over a grave, originating on the Pontic–Caspian steppe and spreading through Central Asia and Europe, with the earliest examples dating to the fourth millennium BC.

marija-gimbutas.name: Marija Gimbutas
marija-gimbutas.summary: Lithuanian archaeologist and anthropologist known for her research into Neolithic and Bronze Age 'Old Europe' and for the Kurgan hypothesis placing the Proto-Indo-European homeland in the Pontic Steppe.

steppe-theory.name: Steppe theory (Kurgan hypothesis)
steppe-theory.summary: The leading proposal that the Proto-Indo-European homeland lay among Pontic steppe peoples buried under kurgan burial mounds, who then expanded across Europe and parts of Asia.

khvalynsk-culture.name: Khvalynsk culture
khvalynsk-culture.summary: A Middle Copper Age culture of about 4900 to 3500 BCE in the middle Volga region, named after the town of Khvalynsk and preceded by the Samara culture.

samara-culture.name: Samara culture
samara-culture.summary: A Copper Age culture dating to around 5000 BCE at the Samara Bend of the Volga River, related to later Pontic-Caspian steppe cultures such as Khvalynsk and Yamna.

talianky.name: Talianky
talianky.summary: A village in Ukraine near the site of a prehistoric Cucuteni–Trypillia culture settlement, the largest known in Neolithic Europe.

vasily-gorodtsov.name: Vasily Gorodtsov
vasily-gorodtsov.summary: Russian and Soviet archaeologist (1860-1945) who, in 1903, identified the Yamnaya, Catacomb and Srubnaya Bronze Age cultures of the Pontic-Caspian Steppe.

donets.name: Donets River
donets.summary: A river of the East European Plain flowing through Russia and Ukraine to join the Don near the Sea of Azov, giving its name to the Donets Basin (Donbas) region.

sredny-stog-culture.name: Sredny Stog culture
sredny-stog-culture.summary: A pre-Kurgan archaeological culture in the Pontic steppe from the mid-5th to mid-4th millennia BCE, named after a Dnieper river islet in Ukraine where it was first found.

sea-of-azov.name: Sea of Azov
sea-of-azov.summary: An inland shelf sea in Eastern Europe linked to the Black Sea, bordered by Russia and Ukraine; it is the shallowest sea in the world.

nebelivka-archaeological-site.name: Nebelivka
nebelivka-archaeological-site.summary: A huge Cucuteni-Trypillian mega-settlement in Ukraine dating to around 4000 BC, covering 260 to 300 hectares and home to perhaps 15,000 to 17,000 people.

eastern-hunter-gatherer.name: Eastern hunter-gatherers
eastern-hunter-gatherer.summary: A genetic ancestry group representing the Mesolithic hunter-gatherers of Eastern Europe, derived mainly from Ancient North Eurasian ancestry that came from Siberia.

caucasus-hunter-gatherer.name: Caucasus hunter-gatherer
caucasus-hunter-gatherer.summary: A prehistoric human genetic lineage found in the Caucasus, ancestral in part, alongside Eastern hunter-gatherers, to the Western Steppe Herders such as the Yamnaya.

deriivka.name: Dereivka
deriivka.summary: An archaeological site in Ukraine dated to about 4500–3500 BC, linked to the Sredny Stog culture; a horse burial once thought to show early horseback-riding was later dated to the Iron Age.

samara-bend.name: Samara Bend
samara-bend.summary: A large hairpin bend of the middle Volga River in Russia, known for a remarkable series of archaeological sites dating from 7000 to 4000 BC.

seroglazovka-culture.name: Seroglazovka culture
seroglazovka-culture.summary: A Mesolithic archaeological culture of the Pontic-Caspian steppe, dating from the late 9th to mid-6th millennium BCE, identified by distinctive geometric microliths.

valentin-sedov.name: Valentin Sedov
valentin-sedov.summary: Russian archaeologist and historian (1924-2004) known for developing an influential theory of the origin of the Slavs based on fieldwork on the Russian Plain.
